paragraphs.source_en: The rain-making and rain-controlling is practised not only by the San but by many African groups, such as the Tswana people in South Africa, by the Songhai in northern Nigeria, the Massai and Kikuyu in Kenya and the Datooga in Tanzania (Palau Marti 1957; Mbiti 1969; Le Quellec 2004). The similarity of this phenomenon may indicate that, as for other similarities all over the Africa, it originated in the prehistoric times. It cannot therefore be excluded that what is documented in the South African rock art and elsewhere in the ethnography was already in use during the Early Holocene. It should also be acknowledged that not all things or phenomena had necessarily changed in time and space, especially when considered crucial for survival. Things fundamental for the prehistoric society could have been purposely protected and conserved in their original form from generation to generation.

paragraphs.source_en: Yet another comparison may be made between the San rainmaking and the Central Saharan rock art and archaeological record. As mentioned above, the rain man has to catch and lead the rain animal. Since this animal could be dangerous, rain men sometimes "charm" (calm) it with buchu, a preparation made from a wide variety of aromatic and even narcotic herbs (Lewis-Williams 1981). It is important to say that sometimes a rain animal had the shape of an antelope, especially eland, or at least a part of it, such as its horns. For some San groups the eland was the crucial animal in the creation myth, in all initiation rites for both boys and girls and it was also connected to the fertility and rain. paragraphs.source_en: whilst the novice is in seclusion, the women mix eland fat with buchu and rub it on her. In the boy's first eland-kill ritual the women pound buchu which, by virtue of its strong smell, causes everybody's brain to experience a state of happiness in which social tension are dissipated (Lewis-Williams 1981). This ethnographic record testifies to the importance of certain narcotic plants in rituals involving the presence, real or metaphorical, of antelope. Regarding the rainmaking rituals, although the animal management occurred in the altered state of consciousness, the idea of controlling an animal by specific plant use is evident.
